```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4)
```

```{r setup}
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(modelcompR))
```

A model written with modelcompR is a set of symbolic equations, usually more
of them than a numerical solver needs and often in a form that no explicit
solver can integrate directly. `mtkcompile()` (called `structural_simplify()`
in older ModelingToolkit releases, and available under that name too) turns
such a model into a small system of first order equations plus a list of
*observed* equations from which every eliminated variable can be recovered.
This article explains each stage of that pipeline, shows how to inspect and
steer it, and then covers the code generation and model transformation tools
that work on compiled and uncompiled systems.

The pipeline follows `mtkcompile` of ModelingToolkit.jl closely:

1. **Connection expansion.** `connect()` statements become equality and
   conservation equations, and the component hierarchy is flattened.
2. **Alias elimination.** Equations that are integer linear combinations of
   variables, such as `x ~ y` or `0 ~ a + b`, are reduced with an exact
   Bareiss elimination; aliases and redundant equations disappear.
3. **Index reduction.** The Pantelides algorithm differentiates constraint
   equations until the system has differential index one.
4. **State selection.** The dummy derivative method decides which of the
   differentiated variables remain states and which become algebraic.
5. **Tearing.** Equations that can be solved explicitly for one variable are
   turned into observed equations; what remains are residuals of algebraic
   loops.

All examples below use the predefined time variable `t_nounits` and
derivative `D_nounits`, and a small helper that prints equations one per line.

```{r}
t <- t_nounits
D <- D_nounits
show_eqs <- function(eqs) writeLines(vapply(eqs, format, ""))
```

## A first compilation

A first order lag with an algebraic output has one differential equation and
one algebraic one. Compilation keeps `x` as the only state and moves `y` to
the observed equations.

```{r}
variables("x(t)", "y(t)")
parameters("tau = 3")
lag <- System(list(D(x) ~ (y - x) / tau, y ~ 2 * x), t, name = "lag")
lagc <- mtkcompile(lag)
lagc
show_eqs(observed(lagc))
```

The result is *complete* (its names are fixed and it can be used to build
problems) and *scheduled* (it remembers how it was derived). Calling
`mtkcompile()` on an already compiled system is an error, because the
information about the original model has been consumed. Observed variables
remain accessible through solutions, for example `sol[y]`.

## Connection expansion

Acausal component models are written with connectors and `connect()`.
`expand_connections()` replaces each connection by the equations it implies:
potential variables are equal and flow variables (declared with
`connect = Flow`) sum to zero. The RC circuit below is the one of the
ModelingToolkit acausal components tutorial.

```{r}
Pin <- connector(function(name) {
  v <- Variable("v", t); i <- Variable("i", t, connect = Flow)
  System(list(), t, list(v, i), list(), name = name)
})
Ground <- function(name) {
  g <- Pin(name = "g")
  System(list(g$v ~ 0), t, list(), list(), systems = list(g), name = name)
}
OnePort <- function(name) {
  p <- Pin(name = "p"); n <- Pin(name = "n")
  v <- Variable("v", t); i <- Variable("i", t)
  System(list(v ~ p$v - n$v, 0 ~ p$i + n$i, i ~ p$i), t, list(v, i), list(),
         systems = list(p, n), name = name)
}
two_terminal <- function(name, par, value, law) {
  op <- OnePort("oneport"); u <- toggle_namespacing(op, FALSE)
  q <- Parameter(par, default = value)
  extend(System(list(law(u, q)), t, list(), list(q), name = name), op)
}
resistor <- two_terminal("resistor", "R", 2, function(u, R) u$v ~ u$i * R)
capacitor <- two_terminal("capacitor", "C", 1, function(u, C) D(u$v) ~ u$i / C)
source <- two_terminal("source", "V", 1, function(u, V) V ~ u$v)
ground <- Ground("ground")
rc <- System(list(connect(source$p, resistor$p), connect(resistor$n, capacitor$p),
                  connect(capacitor$n, source$n), connect(capacitor$n, ground$g)),
             t, systems = list(resistor, capacitor, source, ground), name = "rc")
expanded <- expand_connections(rc)
length(equations(expanded))
show_eqs(tail(equations(expanded), 6))
```

The four connections produced six equations; together with the component
equations there are 20 equations in 20 unknowns. `mtkcompile()` calls
`expand_connections()` and `flatten()` itself, and reduces the circuit to the
single capacitor voltage.

```{r}
rcc <- mtkcompile(rc)
rcc
show_eqs(full_equations(rcc))
sol <- solve(ODEProblem(rcc, list(rcc$capacitor$v ~ 0), c(0, 4)), Tsit5())
c(computed = tail(sol[rcc$capacitor$v], 1), exact = 1 - exp(-2))
```

`full_equations()` substitutes the observed equations into the remaining
ones, which shows the familiar `dv/dt = (V - v) / (R C)`.

## Alias elimination

Most of the 19 eliminated variables above were *aliases*: variables equal to
another variable or its negative. Alias elimination works on the equations
whose terms are integer multiples of variables, and it detects redundancy
exactly. In the flat version of the circuit below, the last equation repeats
the conservation law `0 ~ is + ir`, so there are ten equations for nine
unknowns. `alias_elimination()` (the pass on its own) removes the redundant
equation, and `mtkcompile()` then balances the system.

```{r}
variables("vs(t)", "is(t)", "vr(t)", "ir(t)", "vc(t)", "ic(t)", "va(t)", "vb(t)", "vg(t)")
parameters("R = 2", "C = 1", "V = 1")
flat_rc <- System(list(vs ~ V, vs ~ va - vg, vr ~ va - vb, vr ~ R * ir, vc ~ vb - vg,
                       D(vc) ~ ic / C, ir ~ ic, 0 ~ is + ir, vg ~ 0, 0 ~ -ir - is),
                  t, name = "flat_rc")
length(equations(alias_elimination(flat_rc)))
flat_c <- mtkcompile(flat_rc)
unknowns(flat_c)
show_eqs(observed(flat_c))
```

When two aliases contradict each other, as `x ~ y` and `x ~ -y`, both
variables are forced to zero and become the observed equations `x ~ 0` and
`y ~ 0`.

## The Cartesian pendulum: an index 3 DAE

A pendulum of length `L` written in Cartesian coordinates is the standard
example of a high index DAE. With the tension `T` as a Lagrange multiplier:

$$x'' = T x, \qquad y'' = T y - g, \qquad 0 = x^2 + y^2 - L^2.$$

The tension appears in no equation that can be solved for it: the constraint
has to be differentiated twice before `T` enters and three times before the
system becomes an ODE, so the differential index is three. Explicit and
implicit ODE solvers alike cannot integrate this form directly.

```{r}
px <- Variable("x", t, state_priority = 10, guess = 1)
py <- Variable("y", t, guess = -1)
tens <- Variable("T", t, guess = 1)
g <- Parameter("g", default = 9.81)
len <- Parameter("L", default = 1)
pend <- System(list(D(D(px)) ~ tens * px, D(D(py)) ~ tens * py - g,
                    0 ~ px^2 + py^2 - len^2), t, name = "pend")
pend
```

### Pantelides index reduction

`dae_index_lowering()` runs the Pantelides algorithm alone (ModelingToolkit's
`dae_index_lowering`). It finds the minimal set of equations to
differentiate and replaces the constraint by its second derivative, which
gives an index one system in which every second derivative and the tension
are determined.

```{r}
show_eqs(equations(dae_index_lowering(pend)))
```

This form has lost the position and velocity constraints; integrating it
lets the pendulum drift off the circle. `mtkcompile(pend, dummy_derivative =
FALSE)` produces this index one system with all four positions and
velocities as states.

```{r}
show_eqs(equations(mtkcompile(pend, dummy_derivative = FALSE)))
```

### Dummy derivatives

The default, the dummy derivative method of Mattsson and Söderlind, keeps the
original constraint and all of its derivatives. To restore a square system it
declares some derivatives to be ordinary algebraic variables (dummy
derivatives). Here `y` and its velocity `yˍt` become algebraic, while `x` and
its velocity `xˍt` remain differential states; the `state_priority = 10` on
`x` decides which coordinate is kept.

```{r}
pendc <- mtkcompile(pend)
pendc
show_eqs(observed(pendc))
```

The five unknowns include two differential states and three algebraic
variables, determined by the position constraint, the velocity constraint and
the acceleration constraint. The variable names `xˍt` and `yˍtt` are the
lowered derivative names of ModelingToolkit (`D(x)` becomes `xˍt`).

### Solving the reduced pendulum

`ODEProblem()` accepts values for any variable of the original model,
including derivatives such as `D(px)`. Here only the angle and the zero
initial velocity are given; initialization solves the constraints for `y`,
`yˍt` and `T`, starting from their guesses.

```{r}
th0 <- 0.5
prob <- ODEProblem(pendc, list(px ~ sin(th0), D(px) ~ 0), c(0, 3))
prob$u0
sol <- solve(prob, Rodas5P(), reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-8)
sol$retcode
max(abs(sol[px]^2 + sol[py]^2 - 1))
```

The constraint holds to the solver tolerance during the whole integration,
since it is part of the equations. The tension `T` is an algebraic unknown of
the compiled system and can be queried like the coordinates.

```{r}
plot(sol$t, sol[px], type = "l", xlab = "t", ylab = "position", ylim = c(-1, 0.6))
lines(sol$t, sol[py], lty = 2)
legend("bottomright", c("x(t)", "y(t)"), lty = 1:2, bty = "n")
sol(3, idxs = list(px, py, tens))
```

As a check, the angle obeys `theta'' = -(g / L) sin(theta)`; the angle at
`t = 3` recovered from the Cartesian solution agrees with a direct
integration of that ODE.

```{r}
pendulum_angle <- function(u, p, t) c(u[2], -9.81 * sin(u[1]))
ref <- solve(ODEProblem(pendulum_angle, c(th0, 0), c(0, 3)), Tsit5(), reltol = 1e-10, abstol = 1e-10)
c(cartesian = atan2(sol(3, idxs = px), -sol(3, idxs = py)), angle_ode = ref(3)[1])
```

## Steering state selection

State selection uses three pieces of information, all of which mirror
ModelingToolkit:

* `state_priority` metadata on a variable, or `state_priorities` given to
  `System()`: higher priority variables are preferred as states and as the
  representatives of alias groups.
* `irreducible = TRUE` metadata, or the `irreducibles` argument: the variable
  is never eliminated, not even as an alias.
* `guess` metadata does not influence the structure; it seeds the nonlinear
  solves of initialization.

```{r}
xs <- Variable("x", t); ys <- Variable("y", t)
show_eqs(equations(mtkcompile(System(list(D(xs) ~ 2 * xs, ys ~ xs), t, name = "swap"))))
show_eqs(equations(mtkcompile(System(list(D(xs) ~ 2 * xs, ys ~ xs), t, name = "swap",
                                     state_priorities = list(ys ~ 10)))))
yirr <- Variable("y", t, irreducible = TRUE)
mtkcompile(System(list(D(xs) ~ -xs, yirr ~ 2 * xs), t, name = "irr"))
```

With the priority, the differential equation is rewritten in terms of `y`.
The irreducible `y` stays an algebraic unknown, so the result is a DAE with
one differential and one algebraic equation.

## Tearing and algebraic loops

After index reduction, each algebraic variable is matched to an equation.
When an equation is linear in its matched variable with a coefficient that
may be divided by, the variable is solved for explicitly. When a group of
algebraic equations forms a loop (a strongly connected component, SCC),
tearing picks some variables as *tearing variables* that stay unknowns and
solves the rest of the loop in terms of them.

```{r}
variables("h(t)", "w3(t)")
parameters("p = 0.3")
w1 <- Variable("w1", t, guess = 1)
w2 <- Variable("w2", t, guess = 0.5)
loop <- System(list(D(h) ~ w1 - h, 0 ~ w1 - sin(w2) - h, 0 ~ w2 - cos(w1) + p,
                    w3 ~ w1 + w2), t, name = "loop")
loopc <- mtkcompile(loop)
show_eqs(equations(loopc))
show_eqs(observed(loopc))
```

`w2` was solved from the third equation, and `w1` remains the tearing
variable of the loop, determined by the residual `0 ~ w1 - sin(w2) - h`. The
compiled system is a semi-explicit DAE of index one. Two tearing algorithms
are available through `tearing_alg`: `"carpanzano"` (the default) and
`"modia"`. On this small loop both make the same choice.

```{r}
show_eqs(equations(mtkcompile(loop, tearing_alg = "modia")))
```

The individual passes are exported for experiments: `tearing()` tears
without index reduction, `dummy_derivative()` reduces the index and selects
states, and `tearing_substitution()` substitutes the observed equations into
the result.

```{r}
variables("q(t)", "r(t)", "s(t)")
parameters("k")
torn <- tearing(System(list(D(q) ~ -k * r, 0 ~ q - r + s, 0 ~ s - sin(q)), t, name = "torn"))
show_eqs(observed(torn))
show_eqs(equations(tearing_substitution(torn)))
```

### Solving loops inside the right-hand side

Two options remove algebraic loops from the compiled system altogether.
`inline_linear_sccs = TRUE` solves each linear block symbolically when it has
at most `analytical_linear_scc_limit` variables (default 2) and with a
numerical linear solve at run time otherwise, as ModelingToolkit does.

```{r}
variables("z(t)", "v1(t)", "v2(t)")
parameters("a = 2", "b = 3")
lin <- System(list(D(z) ~ -z + v1, a * v1 + v2 ~ z, v1 - b * v2 ~ sin(t)), t, name = "lin")
show_eqs(equations(mtkcompile(lin)))
lin_inline <- mtkcompile(lin, inline_linear_sccs = TRUE)
show_eqs(equations(lin_inline))
show_eqs(observed(lin_inline))
```

`inline_nonlinear_sccs = TRUE` is an extension of modelcompR: each torn
nonlinear block is solved by a nested Newton iteration in the generated
right-hand side. The DAE becomes an ODE, which an explicit method such as
`Tsit5()` can integrate.

```{r}
loop_ode <- mtkcompile(loop, inline_nonlinear_sccs = TRUE)
show_eqs(observed(loop_ode))
s_ode <- solve(ODEProblem(loop_ode, list(h ~ 0.5), c(0, 2)), Tsit5(), reltol = 1e-10, abstol = 1e-10)
s_dae <- solve(ODEProblem(loopc, list(h ~ 0.5), c(0, 2)), Rodas5P(), reltol = 1e-10, abstol = 1e-10)
rbind(ode = s_ode(2, idxs = list(h, w1, w2, w3)), dae = s_dae(2, idxs = list(h, w1, w2, w3)))
```

## Which coefficients may be divided by

Solving `0 ~ c * v + rest` for `v` divides by `c`, which is only safe when
`c` cannot vanish. Three options, documented under `?mtkcompile_options`,
control this:

* `allow_symbolic` (default `FALSE`): also divide by coefficients that
  contain unknowns.
* `allow_parameter` (default `TRUE`): divide by coefficients that contain
  parameters. A parameter whose default value is zero is never divided by.
* `conservative` (default `FALSE`): for numeric coefficients, only divide by
  1 and -1.

```{r}
variables("e1(t)", "e2(t)")
parameters("kk")
show_eqs(equations(mtkcompile(System(list(D(e1) ~ -e1, 0 ~ e1 * e2 - 1), t, name = "c1"))))
show_eqs(observed(mtkcompile(System(list(D(e1) ~ -e1, 0 ~ e1 * e2 - 1), t, name = "c1"),
                             allow_symbolic = TRUE)))
show_eqs(equations(mtkcompile(System(list(D(e1) ~ -e1, 0 ~ kk * e2 - e1), t, name = "c2"),
                              allow_parameter = FALSE)))
show_eqs(equations(mtkcompile(System(list(D(e1) ~ -e1, 0 ~ e1 + 2 * e2), t, name = "c3"),
                              conservative = TRUE)))
```

In the last case the coefficient 2 of `e2` is not 1 or -1, so the equation
stays a residual. In this implementation `conservative` only restricts
numeric coefficients; a parameter coefficient such as `kk` is still divided
by unless `allow_parameter = FALSE`.

## Other options of mtkcompile

**Balance checks.** By default the system must have as many equations as
highest order variables. Violations raise conditions with the class names of
ModelingToolkit, listing the likely culprits. `fully_determined = FALSE`
skips the check and keeps surplus variables as unknowns.

```{r}
variables("f1(t)", "f2(t)")
err <- tryCatch(mtkcompile(System(list(D(f1) ~ f1 + f2), t, name = "under")), error = identity)
class(err)[1]
err <- tryCatch(mtkcompile(System(list(D(f1) ~ f2, 0 ~ f1 + 1, 0 ~ f1 - 2), t, name = "over")),
                error = identity)
cat(conditionMessage(err))
unknowns(mtkcompile(System(list(D(f1) ~ f1 + f2), t, name = "under"), fully_determined = FALSE))
```

Structurally singular systems (balanced, but with no perfect matching) raise
`InvalidSystemException`.

**Zero derivatives.** With `eliminate_mm_zeros = TRUE`, a state with
`D(x) ~ 0` is integrated analytically to the observed `x ~ x#0`, where the
new parameter `x#0` is solved for at initialization. This is ModelingToolkit's
default behavior; modelcompR keeps such states by default.

```{r}
variables("m1(t)", "m2(t)")
mtkcompile(System(list(D(m1) ~ 0, D(m2) ~ m1), t, name = "int"), eliminate_mm_zeros = TRUE)
```

**Simplification.** `simplify = TRUE` simplifies the resulting expressions.

```{r}
show_eqs(equations(mtkcompile(System(list(D(m1) ~ (m1^2 - 1) / (m1 - 1)), t, name = "s"),
                              simplify = TRUE)))
```

**Base pipeline.** `structural = FALSE` runs only the simpler
ModelingToolkitBase pipeline: higher order derivatives are lowered and
trivially solvable observed equations removed, without alias elimination,
index reduction or tearing.

```{r}
mtkcompile(System(list(D(D(m1)) ~ -m1, m2 ~ 2 * m1), t, name = "osc"), structural = FALSE)
```

**Additional passes.** `additional_passes` is a list of functions applied to
the compiled system. `IfLifting` is one such pass: it replaces conditions in
the equations by discrete parameters switched by events, so that the solver
stops exactly at each discontinuity.

```{r}
variables("l1(t)", "l2(t)")
mtkcompile(System(list(D(l1) ~ abs(l2), l2 ~ sin(t)), t, name = "abs"),
           additional_passes = list(IfLifting))
```

## Mass matrix DAEs and DAEProblem

A compiled system with algebraic equations is an index one DAE in
semi-explicit form, `M u' = f(u, p, t)`, whose mass matrix `M` has a zero row
for each algebraic equation. `ODEProblem()` builds a mass matrix problem, the
form ModelingToolkit uses by default; it is solved by Rosenbrock methods such
as `Rodas5P()` and by BDF methods such as `FBDF()`.

```{r}
da <- Variable("a", t)
db <- Variable("b", t, guess = 0.5)
dc <- Parameter("c", default = 1)
dae1 <- mtkcompile(System(list(D(da) ~ -da + db, 0 ~ db^3 + db - dc * da), t, name = "dae1"))
calculate_massmatrix(dae1)
pm <- ODEProblem(dae1, list(da ~ 1), c(0, 3))
pm$u0
sm <- solve(pm, Rodas5P(), reltol = 1e-10, abstol = 1e-10)
sm(3, idxs = list(da, db))
```

The algebraic unknown `b` had no value; initialization solved
`b^3 + b = 1` from the guess 0.5.

`DAEProblem()` builds the fully implicit form `F(u', u, p, t) = 0`
(ModelingToolkit's `DAEProblem`), solved by `DFBDF()` or `DImplicitEuler()`.
Initial derivatives are given as `D(x) ~ value`, and `differential_vars`
records which unknowns have derivatives. Before solving, `u0` holds the
guess for `b` and `du0` the given derivative; the solver computes consistent
values at the first step.

```{r}
pd <- DAEProblem(dae1, list(da ~ 1, D(da) ~ -0.3), c(0, 3))
rbind(u0 = pd$u0, du0 = pd$du0)
pd$differential_vars
sd <- solve(pd, DFBDF(), reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-8)
sd(c(0, 3), idxs = list(da, db))
```

Both forms give the same trajectory. The mass matrix form is usually faster
for semi-explicit systems and lets every Rosenbrock or BDF method be used,
while the implicit form is the natural target for fully implicit solvers.
`DAEFunction(sys, jac = TRUE)` also generates the iteration matrix
`dF/du + gamma dF/du'` as a function of `(du, u, p, gamma, t)`.

```{r}
dfun <- DAEFunction(dae1, jac = TRUE)
dfun$jac(c(-0.3, 0), c(1, 0.68), 1, 10, 0)
```

## Inspecting a compiled system

Besides `unknowns()`, `equations()`, `observed()` and `full_equations()`,
several accessors describe the result:

* `observables(sys)`: the left-hand sides of the observed equations;
* `diff_equations(sys)` and `alg_equations(sys)`: the two kinds of
  equations;
* `calculate_massmatrix(sys)`: the mass matrix;
* `get_schedule(sys)`: the order in which the algebraic blocks are solved;
* `get_tearing_state(sys)`: the structural state after compilation.

```{r}
observables(pendc)
show_eqs(alg_equations(pendc))
get_schedule(pendc)$var_sccs
```

The structural information itself lives in a `TearingState`, the object the
whole pipeline operates on. Built from the original pendulum, it lists every
variable together with the derivative chain linking it to its derivative,
the variable-equation incidence graph and, after `find_solvables()`, the
subgraph of pairs where the equation can be solved for the variable.

```{r}
ts <- TearingState(pend)
ts
ts$structure$graph
find_solvables(ts)
ts$structure$solvable_graph
highest_order_variable_mask(ts)(seq_along(ts$fullvars))
```

Only the second derivatives and the tension are highest order variables;
those are the ones the equations must determine. The incidence helpers of
ModelingToolkit are available as well: `sorted_incidence_matrix()` gives the
incidence of the compiled system with rows and columns in solve order (the
columns are the variables of its tearing state), `but_ordered_incidence()`
the block upper triangular incidence of the highest order variables, and
`map_variables_to_equations()` the equation that determines each variable.

```{r}
sorted_incidence_matrix(pendc)
show_eqs(get_tearing_state(pendc)$fullvars)
bt <- but_ordered_incidence(TearingState(pend))
bt[[1]]
vmap <- map_variables_to_equations(pendc)
writeLines(paste(names(vmap), "<-", vapply(vmap, format, "")))
```

`asgraph()`, `equation_dependencies()`, `variable_dependencies()`,
`eqeq_dependencies()` and `varvar_dependencies()` build the dependency
graphs of ModelingToolkit's dependency graph utilities, for example to find
which equations share variables.

```{r}
asgraph(pend)
```

## Debugging a model

`debug_system()` wraps calls to functions with restricted domains (by
default `log`, `sqrt`, `^`, `/`, `inv`, `asin` and `acos`) so that the first
call that produces a non-finite value stops the simulation with a message
naming the call and its inputs. The model below drains two tanks with
`D(u) ~ -sqrt(u)`, which reaches zero in finite time; the solver then
evaluates the square root of a slightly negative level.

```{r}
u1 <- Variable("u1", t); u2 <- Variable("u2", t)
tanks <- System(list(D(u1) ~ -sqrt(u1), D(u2) ~ -sqrt(u2)), t,
                initial_conditions = list(u1 ~ 1, u2 ~ 2), name = "tanks")
dtanks <- debug_system(mtkcompile(tanks), functions = "sqrt")
res <- tryCatch(solve(ODEProblem(dtanks, list(), c(0, 10))), error = conditionMessage)
cat(res)
```

**Assertions** are conditions attached to a system with `assertions =
list(list(condition, message))`. While an assertion fails, the generated
right-hand side returns `NaN`, so the solver rejects the step and stops if it
cannot avoid the region. The warning below is the expected outcome.

```{r}
atanks <- System(list(D(u1) ~ -sqrt(u1), D(u2) ~ -sqrt(u2)), t,
                 initial_conditions = list(u1 ~ 1, u2 ~ 2), name = "tanks",
                 assertions = list(list(u1 + u2 >= 2, "the tanks hold less than 2 units")))
atanksc <- mtkcompile(atanks)
asol <- withCallingHandlers(solve(ODEProblem(atanksc, list(), c(0, 10)), Tsit5()),
                            warning = function(w) {
                              message("warning: ", conditionMessage(w))
                              invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
                            })
asol$retcode
tail(asol$t, 1)
```

`debug_system()` also enables the messages of failing assertions through the
parameter `ASSERTION_LOG_VARIABLE` (value 1 by default; set it to 0 with
`remake()` to silence them).

```{r}
dprob <- ODEProblem(debug_system(atanksc, functions = character()), list(), c(0, 10))
msgs <- character()
invisible(withCallingHandlers(suppressWarnings(solve(dprob, Tsit5(), dtmin = 0.1)),
                              message = function(m) {
                                msgs <<- c(msgs, conditionMessage(m))
                                invokeRestart("muffleMessage")
                              }))
cat(msgs[1])
```

## Inputs, outputs and disturbances

Variables can be marked as inputs, outputs or disturbances with metadata.
Passing `inputs` to `mtkcompile()` turns those variables into parameters
of the compiled system, so their values are supplied from outside; `outputs`
are kept available as observed variables; `disturbance_inputs` are treated
like inputs. This is how ModelingToolkit prepares models for control design.

```{r}
cx <- Variable("x", t)
cu <- Variable("u", t, input = TRUE)
cy <- Variable("y", t, output = TRUE)
cd <- Variable("d", t, disturbance = TRUE)
ck <- Parameter("k")
plant <- System(list(D(cx) ~ -ck * cx + 2 * cu + cd, cy ~ 2 * cx), t, name = "plant")
c(isinput(cu), isoutput(cy), isdisturbance(cd))
unbound_inputs(plant)
io <- mtkcompile(plant, inputs = list(cu), outputs = list(cy), disturbance_inputs = list(cd))
io
```

`unbound_inputs()` lists the inputs not driven by any equation; once a
parent model connects an equation to an input, `is_bound()` is `TRUE` and the
input disappears from that list (`bound_inputs()`, `bound_outputs()` and
`unbound_outputs()` are the companions).

`generate_control_function()` compiles the system with the given inputs and
returns the function `f(x, u, p, t)` of ModelingToolkit, together with the
order of its states `dvs` and parameters `ps`. Unknown disturbances are set
to zero; disturbances given as `known_disturbance_inputs` become an extra
argument `w`. With `implicit_dae = TRUE` the function is the residual
`f(dx, x, u, p, t)`.

```{r}
cf <- generate_control_function(plant, list(cu), list(cd))
cf$dvs
cf$ps
cf$f(1, 0.5, 3, 0)
calculate_control_jacobian(cf$io_sys)
generate_control_jacobian(cf$io_sys)(1, 3, 0)
cfw <- generate_control_function(plant, list(cu), list(), known_disturbance_inputs = list(cd))
cfw$f(1, 0.5, 3, 0, 0.25)
```

With `x = 1`, `u = 0.5` and `k = 3` the derivative is `-3 + 1 = -2`, and the
known disturbance adds `0.25`. The empty list given as `disturbance_inputs` in
the last call matters: by default every variable with `disturbance = TRUE`
metadata is an unknown disturbance and is set to zero, even when it is also
listed in `known_disturbance_inputs`. The control Jacobian is the derivative of the
right-hand side with respect to the inputs, here the input and the
disturbance.

## Code generation

Every numerical problem is built from R functions generated from the
symbolic equations. They can also be generated directly, which is useful for
custom solvers or for checking derivatives. The functions take `(u, p, t)`
with the state and parameter vectors in the order of `unknowns(sys)` and
`parameters(sys)`. That order is chosen by the compiler and need not be the
declaration order, as the Lorenz system shows; it is safest to take the
vectors from a problem. The result is a plain vector in the order of
`unknowns(sys)`; names that R carries over from a named input vector do not
label the entries reliably, so they are dropped here with `unname()`.

```{r}
variables("lx(t)", "ly(t)", "lz(t)")
parameters("sigma = 10", "rho = 28", "beta = 8/3")
lorenz <- mtkcompile(System(list(D(lx) ~ sigma * (ly - lx), D(ly) ~ lx * (rho - lz) - ly,
                                 D(lz) ~ lx * ly - beta * lz), t, name = "lorenz"))
vapply(unknowns(lorenz), format, "")
lprob <- ODEProblem(lorenz, list(lx ~ 1, ly ~ 2, lz ~ 3), c(0, 1))
lprob$u0
f <- generate_rhs(lorenz)
f
unname(f(lprob$u0, lprob$p, 0))
calculate_jacobian(lorenz)
generate_jacobian(lorenz)(lprob$u0, lprob$p, 0)
```

`calculate_tgrad()` and `calculate_paramjac()` give the partial derivatives
with respect to time and parameters, and `generate_tgrad()` and
`generate_paramjac()` compile them. A forced decay has a nonzero time
gradient:

```{r}
fx <- Variable("x", t); fk <- Parameter("k", default = 1)
forced <- mtkcompile(System(list(D(fx) ~ -fk * fx + sin(t)), t, name = "forced"))
calculate_tgrad(forced)
calculate_paramjac(forced)
generate_tgrad(forced)(1, 1, 0)
```

`ODEFunction(sys, jac = TRUE, tgrad = TRUE)` bundles the right-hand side, the
Jacobian, the time gradient and the mass matrix, and `ODEProblem(sys, op,
tspan, jac = TRUE)` passes the symbolic Jacobian to implicit solvers instead
of finite differences.

```{r}
ofun <- ODEFunction(lorenz, jac = TRUE, tgrad = TRUE)
names(ofun)
ljprob <- ODEProblem(lorenz, list(lx ~ 1, ly ~ 2, lz ~ 3), c(0, 1), jac = TRUE)
solve(ljprob, Rodas5P())(1)
```

Arbitrary expressions of a system's variables, including observed ones,
compile with `build_explicit_observed_function()` (also called
`generate_custom_function()`). For expressions outside any system,
`build_function()` plays the role of Symbolics' `build_function`; with
`expression = TRUE` it returns the generated code.

```{r}
obs <- build_explicit_observed_function(lorenz, list(lx + ly, lx * lz))
unname(obs(lprob$u0, lprob$p, 0))
bx <- Symbol("bx"); by <- Symbol("by"); bk <- Symbol("bk")
bf <- build_function(list(bx^2 + bk, sin(by)), list(bx, by), bk)
bf(c(2, 0), 3)
build_function(list(bx^2 + bk, sin(by)), list(bx, by), bk, expression = TRUE)
```

**Sparsity.** The structural sparsity of a model is visible in its
incidence matrix, and the numerical sparsity pattern of a generated
right-hand side can be obtained by tracing it with `jacobian_sparsity()`
(the analog of SparseConnectivityTracer). `column_coloring()` then groups
the columns that can share one directional derivative.

```{r}
variables("c1(t)", "c2(t)", "c3(t)")
chain <- mtkcompile(System(list(D(c1) ~ -c1, D(c2) ~ c1 - c2, D(c3) ~ c2 - c3), t, name = "chain"))
cprob <- ODEProblem(chain, list(c1 ~ 1, c2 ~ 0, c3 ~ 0), c(0, 1))
fc <- generate_rhs(chain)
S <- jacobian_sparsity(function(u) fc(u, cprob$p, 0), cprob$u0)
S
column_coloring(S)
```

The rows and columns follow `unknowns(chain)`, here `c3, c2, c1`.

## Model transformations

The functions in this section rewrite a system into another system with the
same solutions in new variables, or with additional quantities. They follow
`basic_transformations.jl` of ModelingToolkit.

### Changing the independent variable

`change_independent_variable(sys, iv)` uses a variable of the model as the
new independent variable. The projectile below moves with constant speed `v`
in `x`, so `x` can replace time; the old time becomes an unknown `t(x)`, and
the derivative `xˍt = dx/dt` appears as a new unknown.

```{r}
px2 <- Variable("x", t); py2 <- Variable("y", t)
pg <- Parameter("g", default = 9.81); pv <- Parameter("v")
proj <- System(list(D(D(py2)) ~ -pg, D(px2) ~ pv), t,
               initialization_eqs = list(D(px2) ~ D(py2)), name = "proj")
proj_x <- change_independent_variable(proj, px2)
proj_x
proj_xc <- mtkcompile(proj_x, allow_symbolic = TRUE)
psol <- solve(ODEProblem(proj_xc, list(proj_xc$y ~ 0, pv ~ 8), c(0, 10)), reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-8)
c(computed = tail(psol[proj_xc$y], 1), exact = 10 - 9.81 * 100 / (2 * 64))
```

The transformed equations divide by `xˍt`, so compilation needs
`allow_symbolic = TRUE`. With `add_old_diff = TRUE`, the equation
`dt/dx = 1 / xˍt` for the old independent variable is added as well.

### Liouville transform

`liouville_transform(sys)` appends the unknown `trJ` with
`D(trJ) ~ -tr(J) trJ`, where `J` is the Jacobian of the right-hand side. In
a probabilistic setting `trJ` transports a density along the trajectory. For
`D(x) ~ -k x` the trace is `-k`, so `trJ = exp(k t)`.

```{r}
lx1 <- Variable("x", t); lk <- Parameter("k")
liou <- mtkcompile(liouville_transform(System(list(D(lx1) ~ -lk * lx1), t, name = "decay")))
show_eqs(equations(liou))
lsol <- solve(ODEProblem(liou, list(lx1 ~ 1, liou$trJ ~ 1, lk ~ 0.5), c(0, 2)))
c(computed = tail(lsol[liou$trJ], 1), exact = exp(1))
```

### Change of variables

`change_of_variables(sys, iv, forward_subs, backward_subs)` applies the
substitutions `forward_subs` (new variables in terms of old) and
`backward_subs` (old in terms of new) using the chain rule (and Itô's lemma
for stochastic systems). Taking the logarithm of an exponential decay gives
a linear equation.

```{r}
gx <- Variable("x", t); gz <- Variable("z", t); gal <- Parameter("alpha")
growth <- mtkcompile(System(list(D(gx) ~ gal * gx), t, name = "growth",
                            initial_conditions = list(gx ~ 1, gal ~ -0.5)))
logsys <- change_of_variables(growth, t, list(log(gx) ~ gz), list(gx ~ exp(gz)))
logsys
gsol <- solve(ODEProblem(logsys, list(), c(0, 1)))
c(computed = tail(gsol[gx], 1), exact = exp(-0.5))
```

### Accumulations

`add_accumulations(sys)` adds, for each unknown `x`, a state
`accumulation_x` with `D(accumulation_x) ~ x`, the running integral. A list
of equations `acc ~ expr` accumulates arbitrary expressions instead.

```{r}
ax <- Variable("x", t); acc <- Variable("acc", t)
show_eqs(equations(add_accumulations(System(list(D(ax) ~ -ax), t, name = "s"))))
accsys <- mtkcompile(add_accumulations(System(list(D(ax) ~ -ax), t, name = "s"), list(acc ~ ax^2)))
asol2 <- solve(ODEProblem(accsys, list(ax ~ 1), c(0, 1)), reltol = 1e-10, abstol = 1e-10)
c(computed = tail(asol2[acc], 1), exact = (1 - exp(-2)) / 2)
```

### Fractional differential equations

`fractional_to_ordinary(eqs, variables, alphas, epsilon, T)` approximates
the Caputo fractional equations `D^alpha x = rhs` by a system of ordinary
equations using an exponential sum quadrature of the fractional kernel,
accurate to `epsilon` on `[0, T]`. `linear_fractional_to_ordinary()` handles
linear equations with several fractional orders. The equation
`D^0.5 x = 1` with `x(0) = 0` has the solution `x(t) = 2 sqrt(t / pi)`.

```{r}
fx2 <- Variable("x", t)
frac <- fractional_to_ordinary(list(1), list(fx2), 0.5, 1e-2, 1)
length(unknowns(frac))
fsol <- solve(ODEProblem(frac, list(), c(0, 1)), Rodas5P(), reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-10)
c(computed = tail(fsol[fx2], 1), exact = 2 / sqrt(pi))
```

The returned system is already complete. The agreement improves as
`epsilon` decreases, at the cost of more auxiliary unknowns.

### Other system transformations

* `convert_system_indepvar(sys, iv)` renames the independent variable, or
  makes a time independent nonlinear system depend on a new one.
* `substitute_component(sys, old, new)` swaps a subsystem for another
  component with the same name and interface, and `isolate_subsystem()`
  extracts the part of a model between two analysis points.
* `respecialize(sys, mapping)` records the class of parameters that hold
  non-numeric values such as functions.

```{r}
tau2 <- independent_variable("tau")
nx <- Variable("xs"); na <- Parameter("a")
convert_system_indepvar(System(list(0 ~ nx^2 - na), name = "ns"), tau2, name = "ts")
sx <- Variable("x", t); sk <- Parameter("k")
model <- System(list(), t, systems = list(System(list(D(sx) ~ -sk * sx), t, name = "part")),
                name = "model")
show_eqs(equations(substitute_component(model, model$part,
                                        System(list(D(sx) ~ sk * sx), t, name = "part"))))
```

The linear state space utilities `similarity_transform()` and
`reorder_unknowns()` work on the matrices returned by `linearize()` and are
covered with linearization.

### Stochastic transformations

Stochastic systems, covered in their own article, have three transformations
of their own: `stochastic_integral_transform(sys, -1/2)` converts an Itô
system to Stratonovich form (and `1/2` back), `Girsanov_transform(sys, u)`
adds a likelihood weight that reduces the variance of Monte Carlo estimates,
and `noise_to_brownians(sys)` rewrites noise equations with explicit
`Brownian` variables.

```{r}
variables("sx1(t)")
parameters("sa", "sb")
gbm <- SDESystem(list(D(sx1) ~ sa * sx1), list(sb * sx1), t, name = "gbm")
show_eqs(equations(stochastic_integral_transform(gbm, -1/2)))
gir <- Girsanov_transform(gbm, sx1, theta0 = 0.1)
show_eqs(equations(gir))
get_noise_eqs(gir)
```

### From numerical code to a symbolic model

`modelingtoolkitize(prob)` traces the R function of an `ODEProblem`,
`NonlinearProblem`, `OptimizationProblem` or `SDEProblem` with symbolic
inputs and returns the equivalent symbolic system, as ModelingToolkit's
`modelingtoolkitize`. Names come from named `u0` and `p` vectors, from the
`u_names` and `p_names` arguments, or default to `x₁, x₂, ...` and
`α₁, α₂, ...`. The symbolic model then gives access to everything above, for
example the analytic Jacobian.

```{r}
lotka <- function(u, p, t) c(p[1] * u[1] - p[2] * u[1] * u[2], -p[3] * u[2] + p[4] * u[1] * u[2])
nprob <- ODEProblem(lotka, c(1, 1), c(0, 10), c(1.5, 1, 3, 1))
lv <- modelingtoolkitize(nprob, name = "lv")
lv
lvprob <- ODEProblem(mtkcompile(lv), list(), c(0, 10), jac = TRUE)
lvprob$f$jac(lvprob$u0, lvprob$p, 0)
rbind(numeric = solve(nprob, reltol = 1e-9, abstol = 1e-9)(10),
      symbolic = solve(lvprob, reltol = 1e-9, abstol = 1e-9)(10, idxs = unknowns(lv)))
```

A mass matrix in the numerical problem turns the corresponding equations
into algebraic ones, and named vectors give readable names.

```{r}
swing <- function(u, p, t) c(u[2], -p["g"] * sin(u[1]))
modelingtoolkitize(ODEProblem(swing, c(theta = 0.1, omega = 0), c(0, 1), c(g = 9.81)), name = "swing")
semi <- function(u, p, t) c(-u[1] + u[2], u[1] + u[2] - 1)
show_eqs(equations(modelingtoolkitize(ODEProblem(semi, c(0.5, 0.5), c(0, 1),
                                                 mass_matrix = diag(c(1, 0))))))
```

Tracing requires code whose control flow does not depend on the values of
the state; `if (u[1] > 0)` cannot be traced and gives an explanatory error.

## Summary

| Task | modelcompR | ModelingToolkit.jl |
|:-----|:-----------|:-------------------|
| Compile a model | `mtkcompile()` | `mtkcompile` |
| Expand connections | `expand_connections()` | `expand_connections` |
| Alias elimination | `alias_elimination()` | `alias_elimination` |
| Pantelides | `dae_index_lowering()` | `dae_index_lowering` |
| Dummy derivatives | `dummy_derivative()` | `dummy_derivative` |
| Tearing | `tearing()`, `tearing_substitution()` | `tearing`, `tearing_substitution` |
| Structural state | `TearingState()`, `get_tearing_state()` | `TearingState`, `get_tearing_state` |
| Debugging | `debug_system()`, `assertions` | `debug_system`, `assertions` |
| Control functions | `generate_control_function()` | `generate_control_function` |
| Code generation | `generate_rhs()`, `generate_jacobian()`, `build_function()` | `generate_rhs`, `generate_jacobian`, `build_function` |
| Transformations | `change_independent_variable()`, `liouville_transform()`, `change_of_variables()`, `add_accumulations()`, `fractional_to_ordinary()` | same names |
| From numerical code | `modelingtoolkitize()` | `modelingtoolkitize` |
